title: System Design — What is system design?

questions.question: What does “system design” mainly ask you to do?
options: Memorize one perfect diagram that works for every product forever without changing.
Choose and combine building blocks under constraints so the product meets its goals.
Only write frontend CSS until the design looks modern enough for users.
Pick the newest database brand because newer always means more scalable.
questions.explanation: no one approach is fundamentally better than others; everything has pros and cons

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
reference.excerpt: The desired outcome is to come up with an architecture to achieve system design goals.

questions.question: DDIA calls an application data-intensive when:
options: The only challenge is parallelizing a single huge numerical computation on GPUs.
Data management (volume, change, consistency, availability) is a primary challenge.
The UI uses more than three colors and must animate every button click.
The team refuses to use any database and stores everything in email attachments.
questions.explanation: We call an application data-intensive if data management is one of the primary challenges

reference.book: Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann
reference.excerpt: We call an application data-intensive if data management is one of the primary challenges in developing the application [1].

questions.question: Which set are the standard building blocks DDIA lists for many apps?
options: Databases, caches, search indexes, stream processing, and batch processing.
Only Photoshop, Figma, and slide decks with no servers at all.
Only punch cards and magnetic tape with no network protocols allowed.
Only one shared Excel file emailed around the company each Friday.
questions.explanation: Store data… (databases) Remember the result… (caches) … stream processing … batch processing

reference.book: Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann
reference.excerpt: Such applications are typically built from standard building blocks that provide commonly needed functionality.

questions.question: FSA’s First Law of Software Architecture is:
options: Always use microservices before you have any users or traffic.
Everything in software architecture is a trade-off.
The newest cloud product is never a trade-off for anyone.
Architecture decisions should never be written down for teams.
questions.explanation: Everything in software architecture is a trade-off

reference.book: Fundamentals of Software Architecture, 2nd Edition by Mark Richards and Neal Ford
reference.excerpt: We learned the First Law of Software Architecture by constantly stumbling across it, and we think it gets to the heart of why these universal truths seem so elusive: Everything in software architecture is a trade-off. —First Law of Software Architecture Nothing exists on a nice, clean spectrum.

questions.question: True or false: If you think you found something that is not a trade-off, FSA says you likely have not identified the trade-off yet.
questions.explanation: If you think you’ve discovered something that isn’t a trade-off, more likely you just haven’t identified the trade-off…yet

reference.book: Fundamentals of Software Architecture, 2nd Edition by Mark Richards and Neal Ford
reference.excerpt: True to our original intent, these three laws seem pretty universal and inform many important perspectives for working software architects.

questions.question: FSA defines software architecture as combining which dimensions?
options: Only the logo font and the homepage hero image with no structure underneath.
Architecture style, characteristics (“-ilities”), logical components, and decisions.
Only the number of GitHub stars on a framework repository.
Only the CEO’s favorite color for the login button background.
questions.explanation: architecture style… architecture characteristics… logical components… architecture decisions

reference.book: Fundamentals of Software Architecture, 2nd Edition by Mark Richards and Neal Ford
reference.excerpt: Architects base their decisions on the realities of their environment.

questions.question: According to Xu’s interview framing, the final diagram matters less than:
options: How fast you shout buzzwords before clarifying any requirements at all.
The design process: clarifying, proposing, defending trade-offs, taking feedback.
Copying a famous company’s public blog post word-for-word without trade-offs.
Refusing to discuss failure modes because interviews are only about happy paths.
questions.explanation: The final design is less important compared to the work you put in the design process

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
reference.excerpt: The problem is open-ended, and there is no perfect answer. The final design is less important compared to the work you put in the design process.

questions.question: Why do companies use system design interviews?
options: To grade calligraphy of boxes and arrows with no discussion of constraints.
Because communication and step-by-step problem solving match daily engineering work.
To force one unique correct topology that every candidate must memorize.
To avoid talking about scale, failures, or APIs entirely during hiring.
questions.explanation: communication and problem-solving skills tested… are similar to those required by a software engineer’s daily work

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
reference.excerpt: The system design interview simulates real-life problem solving where two co-workers collaborate on an ambiguous problem and come up with a solution that meets their goals.
